summary: This informational memo defines MIB objects for the Dynamic Authorization Server side of RADIUS, which supports the dynamic authorization extensions defined in RFC 3576. It lets management stations monitor those server functions.

plainLanguage.summary: Sometimes the doorman gets an order to change a visitor's access mid-visit. This is a dashboard for watching the side that receives and acts on those orders.

subtitle: Management objects for RADIUS Dynamic Authorization Server side.

tldr.problem: Network access servers implementing the Dynamic Authorization Server need effective management and monitoring of their Disconnect and Change-of-Authorization message processing.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a MIB module with scalar objects and a client table that allows SNMP management stations to monitor RADIUS Dynamic Authorization Server activity for each Dynamic Authorization Client.
tldr.outcome: This MIB complements existing RADIUS server MIBs and the Dynamic Authorization Client MIB, providing comprehensive management of real-time access policy enforcement.

today: RFC 4673 is an Informational RFC that remains current and unchanged. It is part of the RADIUS MIB family and provides essential management capabilities for RADIUS Dynamic Authorization Server implementations on network access servers.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This RFC defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for the RADIUS Dynamic Authorization Server (DAS), which implements the server side of the Dynamic Authorization Extensions defined in RFC 3576.

The Dynamic Authorization Server component resides on a network access server (NAS) and processes Disconnect-Request and Change-of-Authorization (CoA) Request packets sent by a Dynamic Authorization Client (DAC). The DAS responds with appropriate acknowledgments or negative acknowledgments.

Effective management of RADIUS Dynamic Authorization Server entities is crucial as operators increasingly rely on real-time authorization changes. This MIB enables network management stations to monitor DAS functions through SNMP, complementing RFC 4668 and RFC 4670 which define MIBs for RADIUS authentication and accounting clients. RFC 4672 defines the corresponding DAC MIB. A NAS typically implements this DAS MIB alongside RADIUS client MIBs. A RADIUS proxy might implement both client and server MIBs if it relays dynamic authorization requests.
sections.plainLanguage: A network access server has a piece that receives orders to disconnect users or change their permissions. This RFC explains how to watch what happens when those orders arrive.

sections.title: Dynamic Authorization Server Overview
sections.content:
The Dynamic Authorization Server (DAS) processes requests from Dynamic Authorization Clients (DACs). The typical architecture places a DAS on the network access server and a DAC on the RADIUS server or a separate policy decision point. However, a RADIUS proxy can implement both DAS and DAC roles simultaneously, acting as a server to one set of DACs while being a client to another set of DASs.

Two types of requests are handled. Disconnect-Request packets cause the DAS to terminate a user session. Change-of-Authorization (CoA) Request packets instruct the DAS to modify a user's access attributes (such as bandwidth limits or allowed services) without disconnection.

This MIB module defines three scalar objects and one Dynamic Authorization Client table. The scalar objects count invalid Disconnect-Request and CoA-Request packets from unknown addresses, and store the NAS-Identifier. Each row in the client table represents one DAC with which the DAS shares a shared secret. The table tracks metrics separately for Disconnect and CoA operations, enabling operators to identify which clients are sending well-formed requests versus malformed or unauthenticated ones.
sections.plainLanguage: The server receives orders from clients. The table tracks for each client: how many orders arrived, how many the server processed successfully, how many failed, and how many had problems like bad signatures.

sections.title: MIB Objects and Tables
sections.content:
The RADIUS Dynamic Authorization Server MIB organizes data in scalar objects and a client table. The scalar objects count globally invalid requests: one for invalid Disconnect-Request packets from unknown addresses, another for invalid CoA-Request packets from unknown addresses. A third scalar stores the NAS-Identifier of the DAS itself.

The Dynamic Authorization Client table contains 27 objects per client entry. Metrics are tracked separately for Disconnect and CoA operations. For each operation type, the MIB tracks: number of requests received, requests with the 'Authorize-Only' service type, duplicate requests, successful acknowledgments sent (Acks), negative acknowledgments sent (NAKs), NAKs for 'Authorize-Only' requests, NAKs for non-existent sessions, user sessions removed or modified, malformed requests, requests with bad authenticators, and dropped packets.

Each client entry includes the client's IP address (IPv4 or IPv6), and the counterDiscontinuity object indicating when counters were last reset due to module restart. For Disconnect-Requests, the MIB counts user sessions removed. For CoA-Requests, the MIB counts user sessions whose authorization was changed. This distinction helps operators understand the impact of each request type.
sections.plainLanguage: The table tracks for each client: how many orders it sent, how many succeeded, how many failed, how many had bad signatures, and for CoA requests, how many user sessions were actually changed.

sections.title: Management and Monitoring
sections.content:
Network operators use the RADIUS Dynamic Authorization Server MIB to monitor the effectiveness of real-time authorization changes. High counts of malformed requests or bad authenticators suggest configuration errors or security issues with a particular DAC. High counts of NAKs for non-existent sessions suggest the DAC is targeting stale or incorrect session identifiers.

For Disconnect-Requests, the count of user sessions removed indicates how many sessions were actually terminated. For CoA-Requests, the count of user sessions changed indicates authorization modifications took effect. Comparing request counts to successful acknowledgment counts reveals which DACs have reliable communication versus those experiencing issues.

The duplicate request counters help identify whether DACs are retransmitting excessively due to timeouts or other problems. The dropped packet counter reveals when requests are silently discarded for reasons other than malformed or unauthenticated packets.

This MIB complements RFC 4671 (RADIUS Accounting Server MIB), RFC 4669 (RADIUS Authentication Server MIB), and RFC 4672 (RADIUS Dynamic Authorization Client MIB). Together, these MIBs provide comprehensive visibility into RADIUS operations on network access servers.
sections.plainLanguage: A network manager can check: Are authorization changes being delivered? Are they taking effect? Is there a particular client having problems? This helps ensure real-time access control is working reliably.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The MIB module contains no read-write or read-create objects, so there is no risk of an intruder altering management objects through SNMP SET operations. However, some readable objects are sensitive. radiusDynAuthClientAddress and radiusDynAuthClientAddressType can reveal the IP address of a DAC, useful for targeting attacks on that authorization system. radiusDynAuthServerIdentifier reveals the NAS-Identifier of the DAS, potentially useful for impersonation.

SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 lack adequate security mechanisms. Even on a network secured with IPsec, there is no control over who can access SNMP objects. The RFC strongly recommends using SNMPv3 with full cryptographic mechanisms for both authentication and privacy (encryption) of management traffic. Deployment of earlier SNMP versions is not recommended. The operator is responsible for configuring the SNMP entity to grant access only to authorized users.
sections.plainLanguage: The client addresses could help an attacker target the authorization system. Always use SNMPv3 with encryption to protect this sensitive information.
